rules.text: Teams of up to six. Pick a team name, the sillier the better.
Phones away. No searching and no texting your clever cousin.
Write every answer down. A guess can score; a blank never does.
Each team has one joker that doubles its points for one round. Play it before that round starts.
Spelling doesn’t count, as long as the answer is clearly right.
The quizmaster’s decision is final. Bribes are welcome, though.

rounds.title: Pot luck
rounds.blurb: A bit of everything to warm up the brain cells.

questions.q: Which letter of the alphabet does not appear in the name of any US state?
questions.fact: J shows up only in New Jersey, and Z only in Arizona.

questions.q: The “Fosbury Flop” is a technique used in which athletics event?
questions.fact: Dick Fosbury won Olympic gold with it at Mexico City in 1968, and it soon became the standard style.

questions.q: Which artist painted The Persistence of Memory, the famous picture of melting clocks?
questions.fact: Painted in 1931, it is surprisingly small, about 24 × 33 cm. It hangs in MoMA in New York.

questions.q: What is the national animal of Scotland?
questions.fact: In Scottish heraldry the unicorn is usually shown wearing a golden chain.

questions.q: How many players does each team have on the pitch in rugby union?
questions.fact: Rugby league uses 13 a side, and rugby sevens, as the name suggests, uses 7.

questions.q: Which spice, taken from the stigmas of a crocus flower, is the most expensive in the world by weight?
questions.fact: Each flower gives only three stigmas, so a kilo takes roughly 150,000 flowers, all picked by hand.

questions.q: What is the name of Agatha Christie’s famous Belgian detective?
questions.fact: He first appeared in The Mysterious Affair at Styles, published in 1920.

questions.q: In Greek mythology, who flew too close to the sun on wings made of feathers and wax?
questions.fact: The wings were built by his father, the craftsman Daedalus, to escape from Crete.

rounds.title: Name that flag
rounds.blurb: Tougher flags this time, plus two flags you’ll have to picture from the animals on them.

questions.mark: “Czechia” also counts. Slovakia is wrong: it has a coat of arms.
questions.fact: When Czechoslovakia split in 1993, the Czech Republic kept the old flag, even though both sides had agreed not to.

questions.q: Which country’s flag shows an eagle eating a snake while perched on a cactus?
questions.fact: It comes from an Aztec legend: the gods said to build their city where they saw this exact scene.
The blue, black and white was first used by an Estonian student society in 1884.
Red and blue are said to stand for the country’s two old political parties, and white for peace between them.

questions.q: Which country’s flag shows a golden lion holding a sword?
questions.fact: The lion holds a kastane, a traditional Sri Lankan sword. Four leaves of the sacred bo tree sit around it.
This design was adopted in 2010. The colours stand for solidarity, peace and courage.
The five slanting bands are meant to show a young country moving boldly into the future.
The four stripes stand for the struggle for independence, the Indian Ocean, the light of freedom and the island’s farmland.

rounds.title: Science & nature
rounds.blurb: From the bones in your ears to the planets next door.

questions.q: Which planet in our solar system has a day that is longer than its year?
questions.fact: One spin takes about 243 Earth days, but one orbit only about 225. It also spins backwards.

questions.q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
questions.fact: Two pump blood through the gills and one pumps it around the body. Their blood is blue.

questions.q: What is the chemical symbol for tungsten?
questions.fact: W comes from “wolfram”, its other name. Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal.

questions.q: Which gas makes up most of Earth’s atmosphere?
questions.fact: Nitrogen is about 78% of the air. Oxygen is only about 21%.

questions.q: What colour is a polar bear’s skin?
questions.fact: Black skin soaks up heat. The fur is not really white either: each hair is see-through.

questions.q: At what temperature are Celsius and Fahrenheit exactly the same?
questions.fact: It is the only point where the two scales meet: −40 °C is exactly −40 °F.

questions.q: Which is the only bird that can truly fly backwards?
questions.fact: Small hummingbirds can beat their wings up to about 80 times a second.

questions.q: What is the smallest bone in the human body?
questions.fact: It sits in the middle ear and is only about 3 mm long.

rounds.blurb: Classical tunes played live, mixed with modern hits spelled out in emoji.

questions.fact: Written for Ibsen’s play Peer Gynt. Grieg himself reportedly said it reeked of cow pats.

It was on Four, the last album the band made with Zayn Malik before he left in 2015.

questions.fact: Some scholars doubt Bach actually wrote it, but it is still published under his name.

rounds.title: Emoji cinema
rounds.blurb: Each line of emoji is a film. Say what you see.
rounds.scoring: 8 films, 1 point each. The quizmaster may give hints.

questions.fact: The mechanical shark kept breaking down, so Spielberg showed it far less, which made the film scarier.
It won 11 Oscars, tying the record set by Ben-Hur.
The DeLorean has to hit 88 miles per hour to travel through time.
Tom Hanks won Best Actor for it, a year after winning for Philadelphia.
The falling green code was reportedly made from scanned sushi recipes.
The fancy version of the dish in the film was designed with the chef Thomas Keller.
The production reportedly grew around 500 acres of real corn for the farm scenes.
Daniel Craig plays the detective Benoit Blanc, who returned in later sequels.

Its Danish name, København, means “merchants’ harbour”.

rounds.title: Which came first?
rounds.blurb: Two moments in history, one question: which happened first? Just write A or B.

B.text: The first iPhone goes on sale

questions.fact: The first YouTube video, a 19-second clip filmed at San Diego Zoo, went up in April 2005.

A.text: Nelson Mandela is released from prison

questions.fact: Only three months apart: the Wall opened on 9 November 1989, and Mandela walked free on 11 February 1990.
Sliced bread was first sold in Chillicothe, Missouri, in July 1928. Pluto was spotted in February 1930.
The Scottish inventor Alexander Bain patented an early fax machine in 1843.
Oreos launched in March 1912, a few weeks before the Titanic sank on 15 April.
Same year! Nintendo started that September, making playing cards, not video games.

B.text: The Aztecs found their capital, Tenochtitlan

questions.fact: Oxford says teaching there goes back to at least 1096, over two centuries before Tenochtitlan (now Mexico City) was founded.

A.text: The last woolly mammoths die out

B.text: The Great Pyramid of Giza is finished

questions.fact: Woolly mammoths survived on Russia’s Wrangel Island until about 4,000 years ago, long after the pyramid was built.

tiebreakers.q: How many bones are in the adult human body?
tiebreakers.fact: Babies are born with around 300; many fuse together as we grow.

tiebreakers.q: On average, how far is the Moon from Earth, in kilometres?
tiebreakers.say: about three hundred and eighty four thousand kilometres
tiebreakers.fact: The Moon drifts about 3.8 cm further away every year.

tiebreakers.q: In what year was the Mona Lisa stolen from the Louvre?
tiebreakers.fact: It was missing for over two years before turning up in Florence in 1913.
